Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Midwife
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Therapy Content: avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy, People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore

Vignette:
Two years ago, in the hospital’s lower-level chemical storage room, the valve on a large drum of industrial phenol cleaner ruptured without warning. The substance hissed and sprayed across the linoleum, filling the narrow aisle with a sharp, chemical stench. Clara stood closest to the leak. She inhaled the vapor, felt her throat constrict, and her stomach lurched violently as dizziness swept over her. When the emergency crew arrived, they moved with frantic urgency, shoving past shelves and pulling at equipment with forceful hands. In the scramble, Clara’s forearm caught the edge of a metal supply cart, splitting her knuckles open. Bright red blood pooled and mixed with the slick, iridescent chemical spill at her feet. She lay on the cold floor, gasping, while paramedics worked with brisk, unyielding pressure to clear her airway and drag her toward the ambulance. In the weeks that followed, the physical unwellness never fully receded. She experienced constant waves of nausea, persistent dizziness, and a heavy fatigue that made even climbing stairs feel like a trial. When she returned to the labor ward as a midwife, the clinical environment felt entirely foreign. A raised voice, the aggressive shoving of a crowded hallway, or the sudden violent impact of a rolling cart sent her heart hammering. She found herself unable to watch blood, whether it came from a patient’s perineal tear, a dropped blood pressure cuff, or the small cut on Thomas’s thumb when he was chopping vegetables. What frightened her most was how quickly her body prepared to relive that storage room, how every unfamiliar ache or sudden noise felt like the ground giving way beneath her. She had come to believe she was a weak person, her body no longer reliable enough to anchor her in the world. She felt she did not know herself anymore, the calm professional who once guided families through birth replaced by someone who flinched at her own shadow. These experiences occupied her days in parallel, neither explaining the other, simply present. Over months, the habit of refusing to make any plans for the future, the automatic agreement to Thomas’s suggestions, and the deliberate shutting down of therapy topics accumulated until they left her isolated in her own clinic. She stopped scheduling holidays, dental appointments, or even the next month’s work roster. If Thomas asked her to visit his sister or take a weekend trip, she agreed immediately, going along with whatever others wanted to feel safe, even when her own reserves were empty. After her weekly sessions, she actively avoided thinking about anything discussed in therapy, forcing her mind toward grocery lists or the weather the moment she stepped out of the building. Nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore; the work that had once defined her purpose now felt like a hollow routine she navigated by instinct alone. The accumulation of these habits and beliefs left her staring at an unbooked schedule on her desk, unable to anticipate what tomorrow might bring. She finally sought help because the silence she had built around her days was growing too heavy to carry, and because she was afraid she would lose her license, or worse, lose the ability to recognize herself when she looked in the mirror. She went to therapy hoping for a way to breathe without waiting for the next poison to come, and for a version of her life that did not feel like a borrowed uniform.
